case_name: Shaurya Alloys and connected matters (batch of 424 writ petitions) v. Union of India & GST Authorities
citation: CWP-34296-2024 (O&M) and connected matters, Punjab & Haryana High Court, reserved 21 August 2026, pronounced 1 October 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Chief Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra and Justice Rohit Kapoor disposed of a batch of 424 writ petitions challenging denial or reversal of Input Tax Credit from purchasing dealers under Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act, where the selling dealer had defaulted on tax payment, filed nil/short returns, gone untraceable, or had its registration cancelled retrospectively. The Court upheld Section 16(2)(c) as constitutionally valid but held it cannot be applied mechanically or in isolation merely on proof of the supplier's default; read with Section 155 and provisions such as Sections 41, 73, 74, 75(12), 76 and 79 and Rules 36, 37A and 88C, officers must examine the genuineness of the transaction, actual receipt of goods/services, and the buyer's documentary evidence before denying credit. The Court laid down 14 detailed guidelines for proper officers across Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh covering notices, disclosure of relied-upon material, personal hearing, cross-examination and reasoned orders, and directed pending proceedings to be reconsidered accordingly with no fresh coercive recovery until fresh decisions are taken.
why_it_matters: Gives GST-registered buyers facing an ITC reversal notice over a supplier's default a detailed, enforceable procedural checklist to demand from the department, well beyond the bare principle that Section 16(2)(c) is valid — officers can no longer deny credit on a GSTR-2B mismatch alone.

case_name: Tata Steel Limited v. Union of India & GST Authorities
citation: Supreme Court of India, Special Leave Petition, final order dated 25 August 2026
holding_summary: Tata Steel had challenged a show cause notice dated 13 June 2025 issued under Section 74 of the CGST Act alleging wrongful availment of Input Tax Credit of about Rs. 890.52 crore for FY 2018-19 to 2020-21; with an equal penalty, the total demand was roughly Rs. 1,781 crore excluding interest. After the Jharkhand High Court disposed of the company's writ petition on 23 April 2026 with liberty to approach the appellate authority, the Supreme Court admitted the SLP, stayed proceedings on 19 May 2026, and in its final order on 25 August 2026 set aside both the show cause notice and the consequential order-in-original, while leaving the department free to initiate fresh proceedings under Section 74 if the foundational facts are properly set out in a fresh notice.
why_it_matters: A rare instance of the Supreme Court itself quashing a large Section 74 SCN (rather than remanding it) for defective foundational facts, giving taxpayers facing similarly loosely-particularised fraud/suppression notices a concrete precedent to seek outright quashing rather than a mere remand.

case_name: Punam Chand Kedia v. Registrar of Trade Marks & Anr. (re: 'HMP' mark)
citation: Delhi High Court, order dated 23 September 2026
holding_summary: The Trade Marks Registry had refused Kedia's renewal application for the 'HMP' mark on the ground that the prescribed renewal period, running from a Form O-3 expiry notice dated 17 September 2015, had lapsed. Justice Vikas Mahajan held that the Registry's own internal dispatch log did not amount to reliable evidence that the O-3 notice had actually been dispatched from the Registry or received by the proprietor, relying on the settled position (Union of India v. Malhotra Book Depot) that the Form O-3 notice requirement is mandatory, not directory, before a mark can lapse. The Court permitted Kedia to file a fresh renewal application within two weeks on payment of the prescribed fee, reviving the mark after a lapse of roughly 26 years on the register.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a mark the Registry treated as long-dead can still be revived if the Registry cannot produce real proof — not just an internal log entry — that the mandatory expiry notice was actually sent, giving proprietors of lapsed marks a concrete evidentiary line of attack.

case_name: Kondepati Ganga Prasad v. Bank of Baroda & Anr.
citation: Madras High Court, order reported 8 October 2026
holding_summary: Bank of Baroda had sought a Look Out Circular (LOC) against Kondepati Ganga Prasad, a personal guarantor of GVR Infra Projects, to prevent him leaving the country over the company's dues, even though the underlying loan account had already been closed under an approved resolution plan. Hearing the bank's review petition against an earlier order lifting the LOC, Justice V. Lakshminarayanan held that a bank manager's letter to the Bureau of Immigration cannot be treated as 'law' capable of restricting the fundamental right to travel abroad under Article 21, and warned that allowing nationalised banks to seek LOCs on this basis could embolden private creditors and NBFCs to seek similar restrictions, leaving debtors 'at the mercy of wolves of creditors.'
why_it_matters: A sharp warning against banks using Look Out Circulars as an informal debt-recovery tool once the underlying debt is resolved, giving guarantors and borrowers a strong precedent to challenge an LOC that has outlived the debt it was meant to secure.

case_name: M/s [Petitioner Slaughterhouse Operator] v. State of U.P. & Anr. (Kanpur Nagar slaughterhouse licensing)
citation: Allahabad High Court, judgment dated on or about 13 September 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justice Ajit Kumar and Justice Garima Prashad dismissed a challenge to a May 2025 District Magistrate, Kanpur Nagar order against a large-scale slaughterhouse operator, holding that a 'petty food business' registration certificate under the FSS Act cannot authorise slaughtering activity beyond the petty-scale capacity threshold (a small daily-capacity cap for large/small animals and poultry). The Court held a full/regular FSSAI licence is mandatory for a large-scale slaughterhouse, and a mere registration certificate is not a substitute or stop-gap for operating above that threshold.
why_it_matters: Clarifies that the cheaper, lighter-touch FSSAI 'registration' route is capacity-capped for slaughterhouses specifically and cannot be relied upon by a growing meat-processing operation to avoid the full licensing regime — a compliance trap for expanding abattoirs and meat processors.

case_name: In Re: Cartelisation in Personal System Products (HP India Sales Pvt. Ltd. & Resellers)
citation: Competition Commission of India, order dated 13 July 2026, under Section 27 of the Competition Act, 2002
holding_summary: The CCI found HP India Sales Pvt. Ltd. and five of its resellers guilty of cartelisation in the supply of personal system products (laptops/desktops) in contravention of Section 3 of the Competition Act, 2002, and imposed a penalty of Rs. 126.87 crore on HP India and a combined roughly Rs. 1.22 crore across the five resellers, taking the total penalty to about Rs. 128.09 crore.
why_it_matters: One of the larger single-company cartelisation penalties the CCI has imposed in 2026, and a reminder that principal manufacturers (not just dealers) can face primary liability for cartel conduct carried out through an authorised reseller network, unlike cases where only the dealers are penalised.

case_name: Ashok Upadhyay v. Union Bank of India & Ors.
citation: Writ Petition No. 2385 of 2024, Bombay High Court, (2026) 08 BOM CK 3641, decided on or about 19 August 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices G.S. Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale quashed a major penalty imposed on bank employee Ashok Upadhyay, whose Internal Complaints Committee had first cleared him of a POSH complaint before the complainant escalated to a body the bank itself called its 'Appellate Authority.' The Court held that a combined reading of Section 18 of the POSH Act and Rule 11 of the POSH Rules gives an employer no power to create or constitute its own Appellate Authority — under Rule 11, absent applicable service rules, the appeal must go to the authority notified under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 — and that the entire disciplinary process was vitiated because it rested on an illegally constituted appellate forum.
why_it_matters: Employers who have set up an internal 'POSH appellate committee' or similar ad hoc appellate body of their own design, rather than relying on a properly notified external authority, risk having any resulting disciplinary action quashed entirely — this is a necessary compliance check for every POSH policy.

case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. Atlanta Infra Assets Limited
citation: O.M.P. (COMM) 161/2026, Delhi High Court
holding_summary: NHAI sought to partially set aside an arbitral award (dated 22 November 2025) concerning the Nagpur-Kondhali section of NH-6, which had granted concessionaire Atlanta Infra Assets a 53-day extension of its BOT concession period for COVID-19 disruption (25 days of full toll suspension plus 28 days of severely depressed toll collection, against NHAI's own grant of only the first 25 days) and had rejected NHAI's Rs. 18.75 crore counterclaim over de-scoped service-road works that the tribunal found had already been resolved by a 24 February 2020 Settlement Agreement. The Delhi High Court declined to interfere under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, upholding both the 53-day extension and the rejection of NHAI's counterclaim as the tribunal's plausible interpretation of the concession and settlement documents.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that a settlement agreement recorded during a BOT concession's life closes that specific issue for good — a party cannot revive a 'settled' claim years later merely by repackaging it as a counterclaim in a fresh arbitration, and COVID-period toll-suspension extensions already granted by a tribunal are difficult for NHAI to claw back on a Section 34 challenge.

case_name: Natwar Parmar v. [Developer] (Bhayandar East project)
citation: MahaRERA, review/execution order, reported 28 July 2026
holding_summary: Parmar had booked a Rs. 29 lakh flat at a Bhayandar East project in 2010 and paid Rs. 18 lakh, receiving only an allotment letter with no registered agreement for sale and no possession. MahaRERA's original order of 24 April 2025 directed the developer to hand over possession, but during execution Parmar discovered the developer — who had stayed absent from the original proceedings — had already sold the same flat to third parties through registered documents. On review, MahaRERA ordered a full refund with interest and separately imposed a Rs. 20,000 penalty on the developer for creating third-party rights over a unit already subject to a pending RERA direction.
why_it_matters: Shows MahaRERA will revisit and convert a possession order into a refund order, years into execution, once a developer's concealment of a competing third-party sale comes to light — buyers whose 'won' possession order has gone unenforced for years should check the property's current ownership records before assuming the order is still capable of being executed as possession.

case_name: Kanwar Raj Bhagat v. Gujarat Hydrocarbons and Power SEZ Limited (re: SREI Infrastructure Finance's claim)
citation: NCLAT, order dated on or about 8 September 2026
holding_summary: NCLAT vacated the admission of a Rs. 1,885.08 crore claim filed by SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. against Gujarat Hydrocarbons and Power SEZ Ltd., holding the Resolution Professional's Information Memorandum was defective because that figure had never been reconciled against a Rs. 241.27 crore loan amount already finally determined in the insolvency of the corporate guarantor, nor against Rs. 38.87 crore SREI had already recovered. The Tribunal separately recognised ACIL/BRS Ventures as a secured financial creditor to the extent of Rs. 38.87 crore by subrogation, and ordered a fresh CIRP process to proceed on an updated, reconciled Information Memorandum.
why_it_matters: A reminder that a Resolution Professional's duty to verify a claim is not satisfied by simply carrying forward a creditor's claimed figure — where a related/overlapping debt has already been finally adjudicated elsewhere (such as in a guarantor's own insolvency), the claim in the principal debtor's CIRP must be reconciled against that finding before admission, or risk being vacated on appeal.

case_name: Union of India v. Hariom Projects Pvt. Ltd.
citation: 2026 INSC 1044, Supreme Court of India, decided 18 September 2026
holding_summary: A High Court hearing a Section 37 appeal against a Section 9 interim-relief order had, after appointing a sole arbitrator, directed that the pending Section 37 appeal itself be remitted to the arbitral tribunal to be treated as a Section 17 application — with the parties' consent. A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Prasanna B. Varale set aside that order to the extent of the remittal, holding that appellate jurisdiction under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 lies exclusively with the 'Court' as defined in Section 2(1)(e), and cannot be transferred to the arbitral tribunal's separate Section 17 jurisdiction even with party consent, since the two are distinct statutory fora whose jurisdiction cannot be interchanged by agreement. The Court left the constitution of the Tribunal and the ongoing arbitration otherwise undisturbed.
why_it_matters: Settles that parties cannot consent their way around the statutory division between a Section 37 appellate court and the tribunal's own Section 17 interim-relief power — a pending Section 37 appeal must be decided by the High Court itself, never handed off to the tribunal, however convenient that might seem once a tribunal is constituted.

case_name: Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India
citation: R/Special Civil Application No. 12175 of 2024, Gujarat High Court, decided 14 August 2026
holding_summary: The Court upheld the constitutional validity of Rule 28(2) of the CGST Rules (corporate guarantees between related parties deemed taxable at 1% of the guaranteed amount) and of Section 15(4) of the CGST Act, but read down the words 'whichever is higher' in Rule 28(2) as arbitrary. The effect: where actual, ascertainable consideration is charged for a corporate guarantee (even below 1%), GST applies to that actual consideration; the 1% deemed value applies only where the guarantee is gratuitous or its value cannot otherwise be determined. The Court also held Rule 28(2), effective from 26 October 2023, cannot be applied to levy GST for any period before that date, and set aside related Section 74 notices for past periods, while confirming that a corporate guarantee given by a holding company for a subsidiary is a taxable supply of service even where no separate fee is charged.
why_it_matters: A major practical relief for corporate groups: GST on intra-group guarantees no longer has to be paid on a flat 1% deemed value where the actual guarantee commission charged is lower and genuinely ascertainable — but groups must still be able to show a real, determinable consideration to escape the 1% default.

case_name: In Re: Adani Enterprises Ltd., Adani Power Ltd., Adani Ports & SEZ Ltd. and Adani Energy Solutions Ltd. (Minimum Public Shareholding proceedings)
citation: SEBI settlement order dated 28 September 2026
court: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
holding_summary: SEBI settled minimum public shareholding (MPS) non-compliance proceedings against four listed Adani group companies — Adani Enterprises, Adani Power, Adani Ports & SEZ, and Adani Energy Solutions (formerly Adani Transmission) — with each company paying Rs. 37.05 lakh jointly and severally with its respective directors, a combined Rs. 1.48 crore, without admitting or denying the underlying findings of fact. Gautam Adani and 13 other individuals settled separately. The probe traced back to a 23 October 2020 complaint, with a show cause notice issued 27 September 2024 and a supplementary notice on 3 March 2025; amounts were paid on 26 August 2026. SEBI retained the power to revive proceedings for any false representation or breach of the settlement terms. A parallel SEBI order the same day found the central allegations against Vinod Adani in the same MPS matter were not established.
why_it_matters: A reminder that MPS non-compliance exposes both the listed company and its directors to joint-and-several settlement liability, and that SEBI's settlement route lets large, high-profile respondents close out a years-long investigation without any admission of wrongdoing — useful context for any company and its board facing a similar MPS shortfall.

case_name: IL&FS Financial Services Ltd. v. SKIL Infrastructure Ltd., Nikhil Gandhi & Ors.
citation: Commercial Summary Suit Nos. 779, 886, 887 and 923 of 2019, Bombay High Court, decided August 2026
holding_summary: Justice Gauri Godse decreed four Order XXXVII commercial summary suits in IL&FS Financial Services' favour for a combined Rs. 848.80 crore (individual claims ranging from Rs. 53.94 crore to Rs. 321.46 crore, each with 9% interest from the date of filing until realisation), directing the borrowers, guarantors and other named parties to pay jointly and severally. Nikhil Gandhi was personal guarantor in all four suits, and SKIL Infrastructure was principal borrower in one and corporate guarantor in the other three. The defendants had earlier been granted conditional leave to defend on condition of depositing the disbursed amounts, but failed to comply; the loan documents, initially impounded for insufficient stamping, were later validated after IL&FS itself paid the deficit stamp duty. Claims against SKIL and Gandhi specifically were kept in abeyance pending their separate insolvency proceedings.
why_it_matters: Illustrates how a lender can secure a decree 'forthwith' under Order XXXVII once a defendant is granted only conditional leave to defend and fails to deposit the required security — non-compliance with a conditional leave order is effectively fatal to the defence, whatever the merits.

case_name: State of Haryana & Ors. v. M/s Faridabad Gurgaon Minerals & Anr. (with connected matter M/s Ganpati Enterprises Slate Mines)
citation: 2026 INSC 690, Supreme Court of India, decided 13 July 2026
holding_summary: The Supreme Court set aside a Punjab and Haryana High Court order that had blocked Haryana's enhancement of royalty and dead rent payable by mining lessees, holding that a lessee cannot claim a vested right to a static royalty rate merely because the lease deed is silent on royalty revision. The Court held the state government retains statutory power to revise royalty rates during the lease term even absent an express revision clause in the deed itself.
why_it_matters: Mining lessees cannot rely on a lease deed's silence on royalty revision to resist a state government's statutory rate increase mid-lease — the power to revise comes from the governing mining/royalty statute and rules, not from an express contractual term, so lessees should budget for revisions regardless of what their lease deed says.

case_name: Central Consumer Protection Authority v. PhysicsWallah Limited
citation: Case No. CCPA-2/94/2025-CCPA, order dated 1 June 2026
holding_summary: Acting on a suo motu case opened after a December 2025 notice, the CCPA (Chief Commissioner Nidhi Khare and Commissioner Anupam Mishra) found PhysicsWallah had run a pre-ticked 'Donate for PW Foundation' checkbox adding Rs. 10 per purchase, active from February 2024 to December 2025, generating about Rs. 2.47 crore in donations from over 21.36 lakh users who had to affirmatively deselect it — classed as 'basket sneaking' — alongside emotionally persuasive messaging nudging users to retain the donation, and a free-course sign-up flow requiring mandatory personal-data disclosure. The CCPA imposed a Rs. 5 lakh penalty, directed PhysicsWallah to ensure no dark patterns operate on its platform, and held that voluntarily removing the pre-selected donation after the notice did not absolve liability for violations already committed; the company was ordered to file a compliance report within 15 days.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a platform cannot escape CCPA liability for a dark pattern simply by removing it once put on notice — remediation after the fact does not erase liability for the period the practice was live, which should push platforms toward proactive self-audits rather than reactive fixes.

case_name: M/s Shyam Beej Bhandar & Anr. v. Suresh & Anr.
citation: 2026 INSC 158, Supreme Court of India, decided 5 February 2026
holding_summary: Farmers who bought groundnut seeds that failed to yield had succeeded before the District Forum (compensation of Rs. 20,000 plus Rs. 5,000 costs each) under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, a result the NCDRC restored after the State Commission reversed it. The Supreme Court reviewed a field inspection report showing only about 50% of pods were fully developed, with semi-development in the rest, and found excessive rainfall and other natural factors had significantly contributed to the yield shortfall alongside any seed defect. On that basis, it held there was no complete deficiency of service by the seller, and ordered that half of the compensation already deposited go to the farmers with interest, with the other half refunded to the seller.
why_it_matters: A seed seller facing a crop-failure complaint is not automatically liable for the full loss merely because the seed had some quality defect — where an inspection report shows weather or other natural factors materially contributed to the failure, courts will apportion liability rather than treat any defect as establishing complete deficiency of service.

case_name: Embassy of Peru v. Registrar of Geographical Indications & Anr. (re: 'PISCO' GI)
citation: Delhi High Court, Division Bench, decided March 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench dismissed the Embassy of Peru's appeal seeking exclusive Geographical Indication protection for the standalone term 'PISCO' as applied to the alcoholic beverage, upholding an earlier single judge's order. The Court held Peru may use and protect the composite GI 'Peruvian Pisco' to distinguish its product, but cannot claim exclusive GI rights over the generic/standalone term 'Pisco' itself in India, holding that geographical linkage cannot override the Act's absolute grounds of refusal and that GI protection is not automatic but must be claimed through a specific, properly scoped application.
why_it_matters: A clear limit on how far a country or producer group can stretch GI protection: claiming a composite, qualified GI (e.g. 'Peruvian Pisco') does not extend to monopolising the underlying generic product name itself, which anyone — including other pisco-producing countries such as Chile — remains free to use.

case_name: Sauraj Singh & Ors. v. M/s Indian Airlines Ltd. (Air India)
citation: 2026 DHC 4055, Delhi High Court, decided 8 May 2026
holding_summary: In a batch of writ petitions by workmen terminated in 1998 challenging a Central Government Industrial Tribunal (CGIT) award that had awarded them only Rs. 25,000-55,000 in compensation for illegal retrenchment, Justice Shail Jain held that Air India's privatisation does not shield it from Article 226 writ jurisdiction where the challenge is directed at an Industrial Tribunal's award and adjudicatory process arising from a dispute that predated the disinvestment — distinguishing this from ordinary post-privatisation employment claims against Air India as a private employer, where writ jurisdiction has been held unavailable. On merits, the Court upheld the finding of illegal retrenchment, declined reinstatement given the 25-year delay, and substantially increased (tripled) the compensation, holding a statutory violation of Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act cannot be cured by token compensation.
why_it_matters: Workers with a pre-privatisation industrial dispute against a since-privatised PSU are not shut out of writ jurisdiction merely because the employer is now private — the key is whether the challenge targets a tribunal's award/process from before disinvestment, not the employer's current ownership status.

case_name: FSSAI enforcement action against Everest Food Products and Creative Bakers and Confectioners
citation: FSSAI orders announced 4-5 October 2026
court: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
holding_summary: FSSAI ordered Everest Food Products to recall a specific batch (batch no. E080668761) of its cumin powder after a sample collected in Goa was found, and confirmed on referral testing, to contain residues of the pesticides Azoxystrobin and Thiamethoxam exceeding prescribed limits, expressly clarifying the finding applies only to that implicated batch and not to all Everest cumin powder products. In a separate, unrelated enforcement action the same period, FSSAI suspended the food licence of Creative Bakers and Confectioners with immediate effect after an inspection found serious hygiene and sanitation non-compliances in its production and handling areas. FSSAI separately flagged a Nestlé dairy whitener sample collected from a New Delhi hotel as unsafe and substandard.
why_it_matters: Reinforces FSSAI's batch-specific recall approach — a single contaminated batch does not, and should not, be read as condemning a manufacturer's entire product line — while showing that licence suspension for hygiene lapses is treated as an independent enforcement track from product-specific recalls.

case_name: M/s New India Assurance Company Ltd. v. M/s Hemkund Duplex and Board Pvt. Ltd.
citation: 2026 INSC 1023, Supreme Court of India, decided 21 September 2026
holding_summary: Hemkund Duplex had claimed Rs. 7,31,31,096.78 plus 18% interest under two fire insurance policies; the NCDRC (order dated 19 November 2024) had instead awarded Rs. 2.4 crore with interest, Rs. 3 lakh for deficiency in service and Rs. 1 lakh in costs. A Bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva allowed the insurer's appeal and set aside the NCDRC award entirely, holding the repudiation was justified because the insured had made false declarations and manipulated its books in breach of policy conditions, and that the NCDRC cannot disregard a statutory surveyor's report in a fire claim without identifying a specific deficiency in that report's assessment. The Court also directed return of the Rs. 50 lakh the insurer had deposited, with accrued interest, and left each side to bear its own costs.
why_it_matters: A strong reaffirmation that a surveyor's report carries real evidentiary weight before the NCDRC, which cannot simply override it without pointing to a specific flaw — and that proven false declarations or book manipulation by the insured can forfeit an otherwise large claim entirely, not just reduce it.

case_name: Carestream Health India Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs
citation: Civil Appeal No. 3440 of 2025, Supreme Court of India, decided 12 August 2026
holding_summary: Carestream had imported 'Dryview 6850 Laser Imagers W/3D' and classified them under CTH 9018 90 19 (other diagnostic instruments); Customs reclassified them under the residuary CTH 9033 00 00, a reclassification upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals) and by CESTAT's Chennai bench (Final Order dated 21 August 2024). A Bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva dismissed the importer's appeal, holding the laser imagers lacked any independent diagnostic capability of their own and so could not fall under 'other diagnostic instruments' — accessories compatible with machines classifiable under several different Chapter 90 headings must instead fall under the residuary heading 9033. The tariff difference between the two headings was 2.5%, producing a differential customs duty demand of Rs. 5,21,616.
why_it_matters: A reusable classification principle for any imported accessory or peripheral device marketed alongside diagnostic/medical equipment: if the item itself has no independent diagnostic function, it is likely to be pushed into the residuary tariff heading rather than riding on the parent machine's more favourable classification, regardless of how it is marketed or bundled.

case_name: Pravin Kumar v. ITC Limited
citation: 2026:CHC-OS:400-DB, Calcutta High Court, Division Bench, decided 18 September 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya and Supratim Bhattacharya dismissed an appeal against a Single Judge's order (6 February 2025) that had granted ITC Limited an interim injunction against 'IJM Gold Stag' cigarettes for infringing and passing off ITC's registered 'Gold Flake' marks and trade dress, and separately rejected ITC's cross-objection seeking a wider injunction, holding the existing order already covered infringement of its registered marks and trade dress. The Court held the mandatory 85% statutory health-warning covering most of a cigarette pack cannot be excluded when assessing deceptive similarity between two packs, and that Sections 28-30 of the Trade Marks Act do not themselves bar the suit or an interim order.
why_it_matters: Confirms that statutory packaging mandates (like the large health-warning area on tobacco products) do not give a competitor room to argue the warning itself defeats a deceptive-similarity claim — courts will assess similarity on the pack as a whole, warning included, not on an artificially reduced comparison area.

case_name: State of Kerala & Ors. v. Lulu International Shopping Mall Pvt. Ltd. (re: Thrissur paddy land reclassification)
citation: 2026 LiveLaw (Ker) 464, Kerala High Court, Division Bench, decided 27 August 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench upheld a Single Judge's decision quashing a Revenue Divisional Officer's order that had reclassified Lulu Hypermarket's Thrissur land from paddy/wetland to commercial use, holding the RDO skipped the mandatory report from the Agricultural Officer required under the Kerala Conservation of Paddy Land and Wetland Act before any such reclassification. The matter was remitted for fresh processing within fixed timelines, with the Agricultural Officer's report to be obtained and considered before any fresh decision.
why_it_matters: A clear procedural checkpoint for any commercial land-use conversion application touching paddy or wetland in Kerala: skipping the statutorily mandated Agricultural Officer report is fatal to the reclassification order, however strong the underlying commercial case for conversion may be.

case_name: Rajesh Uttamchandani v. [Liquidator], Syska E-Retails LLP
citation: NCLAT, Principal Bench, order reported on or about 3 October 2026
holding_summary: Syska E-Retails LLP's CIRP (commenced 17 June 2025 on Canara Bank's Section 7 petition) reached its extended deadline of 25 November 2025 without a compliant resolution plan. At its seventh CoC meeting (10 December 2025), neither a 90-day extension nor initiation of liquidation secured the required 66% voting share, and the CIRP expired on 14 December 2025 without a valid extension or an approved plan. A Bench of Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma, Arun Baroka and Indevar Pandey dismissed suspended partner Rajesh Uttamchandani's appeal against the resulting NCLT Mumbai liquidation order, holding that a failed CoC vote on a separate liquidation proposal, or expressions of interest received only after the deadline, cannot revive an expired CIRP — once the statutory period lapses without a plan or valid extension, Section 33(1)(a)'s liquidation consequence is automatically attracted, and a vote on liquidation itself was never a condition precedent to that statutory consequence.
why_it_matters: A sharp reminder that liquidation under Section 33(1)(a) is not something the CoC can vote to avoid or delay by deadlock — once the CIRP clock runs out without an approved plan, liquidation follows automatically regardless of how the CoC's own vote on liquidation itself turned out.

case_name: WVEPL v. National Highways Authority of India
citation: Arbitral award dated 21 September 2026 (disclosed via Cube Highways Trust NSE filing, 22 September 2026)
holding_summary: WVEPL, a toll-road concessionaire and part of the Cube Highways Trust InvIT's first tranche, had invoked arbitration against NHAI seeking modification of its concession period. The tribunal held WVEPL is entitled to a 1,423-day extension of its concession period, and separately held that NHAI's own proposal to cut the concession period by 1.5 years was invalid and not binding on WVEPL.
why_it_matters: A large concession-period adjustment in WVEPL's favour and a rejection of NHAI's own proposed reduction — a useful data point for other InvIT-held toll concessionaires assessing their own concession-period claims against NHAI, though note this is the tribunal's award as disclosed by the concessionaire itself; NHAI's response or any challenge was not available at time of writing.

case_name: Star Grain and Shipping (P.) Ltd. v. Chetan Dalal
citation: [2026] 185 taxmann.com 530 (Bombay), Bombay High Court
holding_summary: In a family-company dispute arising from a company incorporated in 1976, Justice Manish Pitale upheld the Company Law Board's earlier findings of oppression and mismanagement against the appellant, declining to disturb the CLB's factual conclusions on appeal.
why_it_matters: A reminder that appellate courts give real deference to the CLB/NCLT's factual findings in long-running family-company oppression disputes — an appeal is not a fresh opportunity to re-argue the facts, so the quality of the evidentiary record built at the original hearing is usually decisive.
